Yes, these things are prone to error. But if these types of flagrant errors are possible (and they are), can we narrow down the cause. Because accountability can be pretty thin when we least expect it.

> Yes, these things are prone to error. But if these types of flagrant errors are possible (and they are), can we narrow down the cause. Because accountability can be pretty thin when we least expect it.

The cause is a limitation of large language models. Saying things like "Do not misinterpret me" is almost inviting misinterpretation, the solution simply isn't that easy. This is practically unavoidable in the context of how large language models function, and this combined with how accountability _can_ wear thin is exactly why we should be reconsidering putting so much trust in them.

> > Yes, these things are prone to error. But if these types of flagrant errors are possible (and they are), can we narrow down the cause. Because accountability can be pretty thin when we least expect it.
> 
> The cause is a limitation of large language models. Saying things like "Do not misinterpret me" is almost inviting misinterpretation, the solution simply isn't that easy. This is practically unavoidable in the context of how large language models function

The only reliable way to actually enforce that it behaves as you expect is by using hooks (https://geminicli.com/docs/hooks/) to validate things and block anything you consider to be dangerous. 

Having said that, LLMs are notorious for figuring out how to work around limitations. For example, if you block using `rm` to delete important files, it might write and execute a Python script to do the same thing. That's why some are sandboxed, but there's things that could be dangerous even in a sandbox.
